lead: Moses tells Israel that God’s law is its wisdom and its glory. Jesus says he has come not to abolish that law but to fulfill it. The Psalm sings the same thing: God has made his word known to Jacob and his statutes to Israel. Lent is a good time to learn that God’s commandments are a gift to those he loves. The key words are statutes, near and fulfill.

r.h: What other nation has a god so near?
set: Deuteronomy is presented as Moses’ farewell, spoken on the far side of the Jordan “in the land of Moab” (1:5), before the people enter the land he will not enter. Chapter 4 closes his first speech. The verses left out of the reading (4:2–4) recall the sin at Baal-peor. Many scholars think the book reached its final shape over a long time, perhaps as late as the exile, and so these words would also have reached a people who had lost the land.
The argument is striking. Israel was a small people among great empires, and Moses tells them that they have what the empires lack: a God who is near, and a law that is just.
str: v. 1: “give heed”: keep the law and live.
vv. 5–6: the law is your wisdom in the eyes of the nations.
vv. 7–8: two questions: what other nation has a god so near, or a law so just?
v. 9: take care to remember, and pass it on to the children.
kw: A standing pair in Deuteronomy, meaning the whole body of God’s instruction for life in the land.

What makes Israel great in v. 7 is not its size but God’s nearness, “whenever we call to him”. Deuteronomy will later say the same of the word: “the word is very near to you” (30:14), and St Paul takes that up in Romans 10:8.
“This entire law” in v. 8. The Hebrew means instruction, such as a parent gives to a child. It is much wider than a code of penalties.
vv: give heed to the statutes and ordinances that I am teaching you to observe, so that you may live
The commandments lead to life. God’s law is not a test set up to catch people out.
You must observe them diligently, for this will show your wisdom and discernment to the peoples,
Israel’s way of living is to be a witness. The nations are to look and say, “a wise and discerning people”. The same is asked of Christian homes among their neighbors.
For what other great nation has a god so near to it as the Lord our God is whenever we call to him?
Prayer is treated here as Israel’s greatest privilege. The Psalms, the Temple and every cry to God rest on this.
make them known to your children and your children’s children
Forgetting is the great danger in Deuteronomy. Memory is kept alive when it is handed on at home.
ch: St Paul lists the giving of the law among the abiding gifts of Israel (Romans 9:4), and he says that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). The Church reads this text with gratitude, as something received from the Jewish people. She adds that in Jesus Christ this nearness of God has taken flesh (John 1:14). The Catechism calls the Old Law the first stage of revealed law, holy, spiritual and good (CCC 1962–1963). It also teaches that parents have the first responsibility for the education of their children (CCC 2223), which is what v. 9 asks of them.

r.h: I have come not to abolish but to fulfill
set: These verses are part of the Sermon on the Mount. They come just after the Beatitudes and the sayings on salt and light, and just before “You have heard that it was said … but I say to you” (5:21–48). Before Jesus deepens the commandments, he makes clear that he is not setting them aside. Many scholars think Matthew writes for a community largely of Jewish Christians, for whom this question mattered a great deal.
str: v. 17: he has not come to abolish but to fulfill.
v. 18: not the smallest part will pass away.
v. 19: least and great in the Kingdom: doing and teaching.
kw: Literally to take down or dismantle, the verb used of the stones of the Temple being “thrown down” (24:2). Jesus has not come to pull the law down.

To fill up, to bring to fullness. It is one of Matthew’s favorite words (1:22; 2:15). Jesus fulfills the law and the prophets by keeping them, by teaching their deepest meaning, and by living out in his own death and resurrection what they were reaching for.

The iota is the smallest letter in Greek, and it stands here for the small Hebrew yod. The keraia, a “little horn”, is a tiny stroke on a letter. The POC’s “വള്ളിയോ പുള്ളിയോ” is a happy Malayalam equivalent.
vv: Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.
“Do not think” suggests that some did think so. “I have come” is the voice of someone with a mission from God. Jesus takes up a position toward the law that only its Giver could take.
until heaven and earth pass away, not one letter, not one stroke of a letter, will pass from the law until all is accomplished.
Strong language for the lasting worth of God’s word. “Until all is accomplished” points toward what Jesus himself will do.
but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.
Doing comes first, and then teaching. It is a word for every priest, catechist and parent, and it goes with the warning at the end of the Sermon (7:21).
ch: The Catechism devotes a section to Jesus and the Law. It quotes these verses (CCC 577) and says that Jesus fulfilled the Law by keeping it in its all-embracing detail (CCC 578). It teaches that the Law of the Gospel “fulfills”, refines, surpasses and leads the Old Law to its perfection (CCC 1967). Jesus is a Jew who loves the Torah, and the Christian who despises the Old Testament has not understood him.

qa: If not one stroke of the law will pass away, why do Catholics not keep the food laws or circumcision?

The early Church faced this very question at the council in Jerusalem (Acts 15), and Mark’s Gospel records the insight about foods (Mark 7:19). St Thomas Aquinas taught a distinction that became standard: moral, ceremonial and judicial precepts (Summa Theologiae I–II, q. 99). The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still binds us. The ceremonial laws reach their goal in Christ, in whom Gentiles are welcomed without becoming Jews first. None of this slights Jewish people who keep those laws in faithfulness to God. The Church teaches that the Old Covenant has never been revoked (CCC 121).
study: Do I think of God’s commandments as a burden laid on me or as a mark of his nearness? Which one do I find hardest to see as a gift?
What in the faith did I learn from my family, and what am I now handing on to the next generation, in words and in the way I live?
